doc.title: Hide Tanaka interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 3, 2014

title: Bass solos, high register and pickups
summary: Seventies bassists such as Stanley Clarke, Vitous and Eddie Gomez played higher so audiences could hear melody; pickups help keep listeners from talking.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Yeah, the bass player — the most important thing is to play bass of course. But okay one of the reasons I really wanted to play bass is I really love the sound. But also at that time, the seventies, there were so many super bass players that came out. Stanley Clarke, Miroslav Vitous, Neils Henning, Jordan [inaudible], Eddie Gomez. So all those players became famous means they began to play in the up high register. So people understand what they’re playing. All the best players playing solos in the low register people don’t know, okay this is a bass solo but just sounds [scats]. But when they started an octave higher, like a cello register while they’re playing bass, in the higher register, people really knew the melody what the bass player was playing. Instead of [scats].
They couldn’t distinguish the difference if they stayed down low.

Yeah most people. And that’s why, especially now, great pick-ups we are able to use. So people can hear very well what the bass player is playing. And also everybody mostly when their solo started people started talking. [scats] So if you play a more distinct sound with the bass people still concentrate to the band the same.
It’s not time to go to the rest room.

Yeah there’s actually a couple of jokes about that. How to get people to talk? Take a bass solo. That’s very neat. I noticed last night when you were playing that when it was time for your solo that you did something different to stand out. Whether it was with a bow or going up high. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-
